title: WHY DID GOD HIDE MOSES’ GRAVE? THE MYSTERY OF A BURIAL NO HUMAN EYES EVER SAW
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD HIDE MOSES’ GRAVE? THE MYSTERY OF A BURIAL NO HUMAN EYES EVER SAW

He led millions through the wilderness, stood before Pharaoh, parted the Red Sea, and spoke with God as a friend. Yet when Moses died, the Bible records something astonishing: nobody knew where he was buried. And the truth behind that mysterious grave may change how you understand death, disappointment, surrender, and the grace of Jesus Christ.
There is something deeply unsettling about the final chapter of Moses’ life.
A man who had spent forty years leading an entire nation toward a promise was finally standing close enough to see it.
He could see the land.
He could recognize the mountains.
He could look across the valleys where generations of Israelites would one day build homes, raise children, worship God, and tell stories about the man who had brought their ancestors out of slavery.
But Moses would not enter.
And then something happened that still leaves Bible readers asking questions thousands of years later.
Moses died.
And God Himself buried him.
No funeral procession is described.
No grieving family is shown standing around an open grave.
No magnificent monument was erected to preserve his remains.
No recorded burial site where future generations could kneel.
Just a grave somewhere in Moab.
And a location nobody knew.
Deuteronomy 34:5–6 tells us:

“So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD. And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day.” (KJV)
Read those words again.
“But no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day.”
Why?
Why would the Lord allow the burial place of one of Israel’s greatest prophets to disappear from human knowledge?
Why preserve the details of Moses’ calling, his confrontations with Pharaoh, his miracles, his failures, his prayers, and even his final words—but leave the location of his grave unknown?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all:
What does the disappearance of Moses’ grave reveal about our own desperate desire to be remembered?
Because buried inside this mystery is a truth that reaches beyond a mountain in Moab.
It reaches into the heart of everyone who has ever served God faithfully and still watched a cherished dream remain unfulfilled.
Everyone who has ever whispered, “Lord, after everything I have been through, why does my story have to end this way?”
Everyone who has ever feared that being forgotten by people somehow means being forgotten by God.
But to understand Moses’ burial, we must first understand the man who was buried.
Moses did not begin his life as a celebrated prophet.
He began as a baby under a death sentence.
Pharaoh had commanded that Hebrew sons be thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1:22).
Before Moses could speak, before he could walk, before he could understand the hatred surrounding his people, his life was already threatened.
His mother hid him.
Then came that heartbreaking moment when she placed him in a basket among the reeds of the river.
Imagine her hands.
Imagine the trembling.
Imagine a mother trying to trust God while releasing her child into waters she could not control.
She did not know the whole story.
She could only surrender what she loved.
And somehow, by God's providence, that child was rescued and raised in Pharaoh’s household.
The boy whom Pharaoh’s command had endangered would grow up to confront Pharaoh himself.
But Moses’ journey was not a straight line from rescue to greatness.
He became a fugitive.
After killing an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew, Moses fled to Midian (Exodus 2:11–15).
The man who would one day stand before kings spent years living far from the palace.
And when God called him from the burning bush, Moses did not respond like a fearless hero.
He questioned his own ability.
“Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh?” (Exodus 3:11, KJV)
Later, he pleaded with God to send someone else.
Does that sound familiar?
Sometimes the people God calls are not the people who feel qualified.
Sometimes the person who will eventually encourage thousands is barely holding himself together.
Sometimes the one who will speak courage into another person’s life is privately wrestling with fear.
Yet God did not choose Moses because Moses was sufficient in himself.
God promised His presence.
“Certainly I will be with thee.” (Exodus 3:12, KJV)
That was the foundation of Moses’ calling.
Not his confidence.
Not his reputation.
Not his eloquence.
The presence of God.
And that presence carried him through extraordinary things.
The plagues in Egypt.
The Passover.
The crossing of the sea.
The wilderness.
The giving of the Law.
The rebellion of the people.
The intercession.
The exhaustion.
The moments when Moses stood between a holy God and a stubborn nation.
But Moses was never the Savior of Israel.
He was a servant of the God who saves.
That distinction matters more than we often realize.
Because even the greatest servants of God remain human.
Even faithful leaders can fail.
And Moses did.
In Numbers 20, the Israelites complained because they had no water.
God instructed Moses to speak to the rock.
Instead, Moses spoke angrily to the people and struck the rock twice.
Water still came out.
But God's provision did not mean that Moses’ disobedience was approved.
The Lord said to Moses and Aaron:
“Because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore ye shall not bring this congregation into the land which I have given them.” (Numbers 20:12, KJV)
That is a painful verse.
Not because God was unjust.
But because it reminds us that a long history of faithful service does not make disobedience insignificant.
Moses had seen God's power.
He had heard God's voice.
He had carried enormous responsibility.
And still, in a moment of anger and unbelief, he failed to honor God's holiness before the people.
Perhaps someone reading this knows what that feels like.
Not the exact circumstances.
But the grief of looking back at one decision and wishing you could undo it.
One angry response.
One compromise.
One betrayal of trust.
One moment when you knew what God required, but chose differently.
And afterward, the consequences did not simply disappear.
We love stories where every mistake is immediately reversed and every lost opportunity is restored exactly as we imagined.
But Scripture tells a more truthful story.
God forgives repentant sinners.
Yet forgiveness does not always remove every earthly consequence.
Moses was not permitted to lead Israel into Canaan.
And that brings us to one of the most emotionally difficult scenes in the Old Testament.
Deuteronomy 34 begins with Moses climbing Mount Nebo.
He was 120 years old.
His journey was nearly over.
From the mountain, the Lord showed him the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Moses could see it.
But he could not enter it.
Can you imagine the silence?

After forty years of leading people through the wilderness, after burying an entire generation, after enduring complaints and rebellion, after praying for a nation that repeatedly tested his patience…
He stood looking at the destination.
And heard that he would not cross over.
There is a particular kind of sorrow in seeing something you have spent your life pursuing and knowing it will not become yours in the way you hoped.
Some people know that sorrow through a marriage that never healed.
Others through a child who has wandered far from God.
Others through a ministry that did not grow, a prayer that received an unexpected answer, a door that remained closed, or a loved one who died before reconciliation came.
And the question rises quietly:
“Lord, was everything I did meaningless?”
Moses’ story answers that question without pretending the disappointment was small.
His work was not meaningless.
The promise was never dependent upon Moses being the one to complete every part of the journey.
Joshua would lead the people across.
God's covenant faithfulness would continue.
And Moses would be remembered not as the owner of the promise, but as the servant of the Lord.
That title appears in the account of his death.
In Hebrew, Deuteronomy 34:5 calls him:
עֶבֶד־יְהוָה — ʿeved-YHWH
“The servant of the LORD.”
Think about that.
At the end of Moses’ extraordinary life, Scripture does not introduce him as the man who defeated Pharaoh.
Not the man associated with the dividing of the sea.
Not the man who received the tablets of the covenant.
But the servant of the Lord.
And perhaps that is one of the greatest honors any human being could receive.
Not that everyone knew his name.
But that his life belonged to God.
Then comes the burial.
The Hebrew of Deuteronomy 34:6 begins:
וַיִּקְבֹּר אֹתוֹ בַגַּיְא בְּאֶרֶץ מוֹאָב
Vayyiqbor oto baggay be’erets Mo’av.
“And he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab.”
The verb וַיִּקְבֹּר — vayyiqbor means “and he buried.”
In context, the traditional understanding is that the Lord Himself buried Moses.

The Hebrew narrative does not explicitly repeat God's name as the subject in verse 6, and interpreters have discussed the grammatical details. Nevertheless, the preceding reference to the Lord and the ancient understanding of the passage explain why God's personal involvement in Moses’ burial has long been emphasized.
The verse ends with these remarkable words:
וְלֹא־יָדַע אִישׁ אֶת־קְבֻרָתוֹ עַד הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה
Velo-yada ish et-qevurato ad hayom hazzeh.
“And no man knows his burial place to this day.”
Notice what Scripture actually says.
It does not say the grave was never marked.
It does not say God performed a miracle to erase every trace of it.
It does not explain exactly how the location remained unknown.
It simply records that no one knew where Moses was buried.
That is the mystery.
And we must be careful here.
Because a powerful sermon can become a dangerous sermon when imagination is presented as revelation.
Many Christians have heard that God deliberately concealed Moses’ grave so the Israelites would not worship his body.
That explanation is possible.
It makes sense as a theological inference because Israel repeatedly struggled with idolatry, and Scripture strongly forbids worshiping created things.
The bronze serpent offers a striking example.
In Numbers 21, God used a bronze serpent as part of His provision for Israelites suffering from venomous snakebites.
But centuries later, King Hezekiah destroyed that same bronze serpent because people had begun burning incense to it (2 Kings 18:4).
Something associated with God's deliverance had become an object of improper religious devotion.
The warning is clear.
Human beings can take something that once directed their attention toward God and turn it into something that competes with God.
A symbol becomes an idol.
A memorial becomes an object of misplaced trust.
A servant receives the honor that belongs to the Master.
Could the unknown location of Moses’ grave have protected Israel from that danger?
Possibly.
But Deuteronomy 34:6 does not explicitly give that as God's reason.
We must not turn a reasonable possibility into a declared biblical fact.
And perhaps that restraint is itself part of the lesson.
We do not need to know everything God has not revealed in order to trust what He has revealed.
Still, consider the contrast.
Moses had been one of the most recognizable figures in Israel’s history.
His name would be spoken for generations.
His writings would shape the nation's understanding of God's covenant.
Yet his burial place remained unknown.
No one could build their faith upon the location of his bones.
Israel would have to continue following the living God rather than depending upon the physical presence of the leader who had guided them.
And this exposes something uncomfortable about the human heart.
We are often more attached to God's instruments than to God Himself.
We become devoted to personalities.
We place spiritual leaders on pedestals.
We assume that a particular person, church, platform, or ministry must always remain if God's work is going to continue.
But Moses died.
And God remained.
The servant's assignment ended.
God's covenant did not.
The leader was buried.
The Lord continued leading His people.
That truth is both humbling and deeply comforting.
Because the kingdom of God does not depend upon the survival of any one human being.
Not Moses.
Not Joshua.
Not a pastor.
Not a ministry founder.
Not a writer.
Not you.
Not me.
God allows us to participate in His work, but we are never its foundation.
Jesus Christ is.
And there is another detail in Moses’ story that deserves our attention.
The New Testament mentions a dispute involving Moses’ body.
Jude 1:9 says:
“Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee.” (KJV)
This is one of the most mysterious verses in the New Testament.
Why was there a dispute over Moses’ body?
What precisely did Satan seek?
How does this incident relate to the burial in Deuteronomy?
Scripture does not fully explain.
Jude's immediate purpose is to contrast arrogant, irreverent speech with Michael's restraint and appeal to the Lord's authority.
Even Michael did not presume to exercise ultimate judgment on his own.
He said:
“The Lord rebuke thee.”
That is important.
We should not build elaborate accounts of spiritual warfare around details the biblical text does not supply.
Nor does Jude tell us that Satan wanted Moses’ body specifically so Israel would worship it.
That theory is sometimes suggested, but it is not stated in the passage.
What we can say is that Moses’ body became the subject of a dispute mentioned in Scripture, and the Lord's authority was decisive in Michael's response.
And then, centuries after Moses died, something extraordinary happened.
Moses appeared again in the biblical narrative.
Not at his grave.
Not in a shrine.
Not in a place where Israel had preserved his remains.
But on a mountain with Jesus Christ.
Matthew 17 records the Transfiguration.
Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain.
There, His appearance was transformed before them.
His face shone like the sun.
His clothing became dazzling white.
And suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared, speaking with Him.
Think about the significance.
Moses, who had once stood on a mountain and received God's Law, now stood in the presence of the One to whom the Law and the Prophets bore witness.
Luke 9:31 reveals what they discussed.
They spoke of Jesus’ coming departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
The Greek word translated “decease” in the KJV is:
ἔξοδος — exodos
Literally, “departure” or “going out.”
It is the word from which we get exodus.
Do you see the astonishing connection?
Moses had been used by God to lead Israel in the exodus from Egypt.
But now he was speaking with Jesus about a greater departure that would be accomplished through Christ's suffering, death, and resurrection.
The first exodus delivered Israel from bondage in Egypt.
Through His death and resurrection, Jesus accomplishes the redemption to which the earlier deliverance pointed.
He frees His people from the condemnation of sin and brings them into the hope of eternal life.
Moses could lead people out of Egypt.
But Moses could not remove the guilt of sin.
Moses could deliver God's Law.
But Moses could not make sinners righteous by his own power.
Moses could intercede for Israel.
But Moses was not the sinless Mediator who could offer Himself as the perfect sacrifice.
Jesus is greater than Moses.
Hebrews 3:5–6 draws the distinction:
“And Moses verily was faithful in all his house, as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were to be spoken after; But Christ as a son over his own house…” (KJV)
Moses was faithful as a servant.
Christ is the Son.
Moses testified to what was coming.
Christ is the fulfillment.
And that changes how we read the entire story.
The deepest message of Deuteronomy 34 is not that a mysterious grave contains a secret we must uncover.
It is that even the greatest servant in Israel’s history could not be the final answer to humanity's deepest need.
We needed more than a prophet.
More than a deliverer from political oppression.
More than a lawgiver.
We needed a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
Now consider another contrast.
Moses’ burial place was unknown.
Jesus’ burial place, however, was known to those who laid Him there.
The Gospels tell us that Joseph of Arimathea placed Jesus’ body in a tomb.
Women observed where He was laid (Mark 15:47; Luke 23:55).
And on the third day, the tomb was found empty.
Not because the disciples had forgotten its location.
Not because nobody had witnessed the burial.
But because Jesus had risen from the dead.
The angel's announcement in Matthew 28:6 declares:
“He is not here: for he is risen, as he said.” (KJV)
Moses died, and Scripture records that his grave was unknown.
Jesus died, and Scripture proclaims that His tomb was empty because He rose.
These are different events, and we should not force them into an artificial parallel.
But together they point us toward a glorious truth.
Moses was a faithful servant who died.
Jesus is the crucified and risen Lord who conquered death.
Moses could not bring himself or Israel into the fullness of God's ultimate redemptive promise.
Christ brings His people into eternal life through His finished work.
And perhaps now we can return to the mountain where Moses stood.
Imagine him looking toward Canaan.
The man who had been rescued from the Nile.
The fugitive from Egypt.
The shepherd in Midian.
The reluctant prophet.
The leader who had carried the burdens of a nation.
The man who had sinned, prayed, wept, persevered, and witnessed the glory of God.
His earthly assignment was coming to an end.
And there was no guarantee that people would preserve his burial place.
Yet there is no indication in Scripture that Moses needed a monument to validate his life.
He had been known by God.
That was enough.
And this is where the story becomes personal.
Because some of us are quietly terrified of being forgotten.
We work until we are exhausted.
We try to build something lasting.
We want our children to remember our sacrifices.
We want our service to matter.
We want someone to notice how much we gave.
And beneath all of it is a question we rarely admit aloud.
“Will my life mean anything when I am gone?”
Perhaps you have spent years serving in a church where nobody seems to appreciate you.
Perhaps you have sacrificed for your family, only to feel invisible.
Perhaps you have prayed for people who never knew you were praying.
Perhaps you have carried responsibilities that others will never understand.
And sometimes, when the room is quiet and the strength has run out, you wonder whether God sees any of it.
He does.
Hebrews 6:10 says:
“For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name…” (KJV)
That promise does not mean every effort will produce the earthly result we desire.
It does not mean every ministry will become famous.
It does not mean every sacrifice will receive public recognition.
But it does mean that faithful service offered to God is not invisible to Him.
You may be forgotten by the crowd.
You are not forgotten by the Lord.
And yet there is another truth we must face.
Being remembered by God is not the same as being approved by Him merely because we have done religious work.
Our hope cannot rest in how many people we helped, how many sermons we preached, how much money we gave, or how faithfully we served.
Those things matter as expressions of faith and love.
But they cannot save us.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
That is why the Gospel is so beautiful.
It does not tell us to build a monument impressive enough to earn eternity.
It tells us to come to the Savior who has already done what we could never accomplish.
Maybe you have spent years trying to prove you are worthy.
Maybe you are exhausted from performing.
Maybe you have been hiding behind ministry, church attendance, and religious language while privately carrying guilt that nobody knows about.
You smile in photographs.
You encourage others.
You post Bible verses.
But when the lights go out and the phone is silent, you remember the things you wish you had never done.
The people you hurt.
The promises you broke.
The secret sins you keep defending.
The prayers you stopped praying because you were ashamed to come back.
And somewhere inside, you have begun believing that God must be finished with you.
But look again at Moses.
His failure at Meribah was real.
Its consequence was real.
Yet the story of Moses did not end with his sin being the only thing worth remembering.
Deuteronomy 34 still calls him the servant of the Lord.
Hebrews 11 remembers him among those who lived by faith.
And at the Transfiguration, Moses appears in the presence of Christ.
That does not erase the seriousness of his disobedience.
It reminds us that human failure is not greater than God's redemptive purposes.
But do not misunderstand grace.
Grace is not permission to remain in rebellion.
Grace calls sinners to repentance.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could become comfortable with the sins that destroy us.
He died and rose so that sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed.
The Greek word often translated “repent” is:
μετανοέω — metanoeō
It means to repent, involving a change of mind and turning away from sin.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling bad because we were caught.
It is turning toward God with a heart that no longer wants to defend what He calls evil.
It is bringing the truth into the light.
It is confessing instead of hiding.
It is trusting Christ rather than pretending we can cleanse ourselves.
And perhaps this is the moment when you need to stop reading as a spectator.
Because there may be something in your life that needs to be surrendered.
An old bitterness.
A hidden addiction.
An unforgiven offense.
A secret compromise.
A pride that has disguised itself as spiritual strength.
A fear of being forgotten that has made human applause more important than God's approval.
What if the Lord is using this story to remind you that your identity does not have to be buried beneath your failures?
What if you stopped trying to make people remember your name and began asking whether your life was truly pointing them to Jesus?
What if you stopped measuring God's love by the doors He allowed you to walk through?
Moses did not enter Canaan during his earthly life.
But the Lord had not abandoned His servant.
And Christian hope reaches even further than the earthly land Moses could see.
Jesus promises resurrection and eternal life to those who believe in Him.
In John 11:25, He declares:
“I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.” (KJV)
That is the hope that changes everything.
Not the preservation of our graves.
Not the immortality of our reputations.
Not the applause of generations who may never know our names.
Christ Himself.
And when that truth begins to settle into the heart, even the mystery of Moses’ burial takes on a different weight.
The Bible does not tell us where his bones were laid.
But it tells us whom Moses served.
It does not invite us to make a pilgrimage to his grave.
It invites us to remember the faithfulness of the God who called him.
And the New Testament directs our eyes to Jesus, who is greater than Moses.
Maybe that is the question we should carry away from Deuteronomy 34.
Not merely, “Where is Moses buried?”
But, “Who is receiving the glory for my life?”
Because you can spend decades building a reputation and never surrender your heart to Christ.
You can become known in religious circles while remaining spiritually distant from God.
You can leave behind buildings, books, money, followers, and memories.
And still miss the one thing that matters eternally.
Jesus asked:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (Mark 8:36, KJV)
That question should stop us.
Not because accomplishments are automatically evil.
But because no accomplishment can replace reconciliation with God.
And there is a beautiful freedom in knowing that we do not have to be the heroes of our own salvation story.
Jesus already is.
You do not have to make yourself unforgettable.
You need to belong to the One who will never forsake His people.
You do not have to erase your past through public success.
You can bring your sins into the light and receive the forgiveness offered through Christ.
You do not have to turn your suffering into a performance.
You can weep before the Lord.
You do not have to pretend that every disappointment makes sense.
You can trust Him even when you do not understand.
And you do not have to reach every earthly destination you dreamed of to know that your life in Christ has eternal significance.
Some of God's faithful servants will die without seeing the full earthly results of their prayers.
Some parents will go to their graves still praying for children who have wandered.
Some missionaries will labor in places where the harvest seems small.
Some believers will spend their lives doing ordinary acts of love that never become public testimonies.
But the worth of their faithfulness is not measured by applause.
It is measured by the Lord they serve.
And for those who belong to Christ, even death cannot cancel His promise.
Romans 8:38–39 assures believers that neither death nor life can separate them from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Moses' grave was unknown to the people who came after him.
But Moses was never beyond God's knowledge.
And neither are His children.
If this story has touched a place in your heart that you have kept hidden, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than simply reacting to a post.
Be honest before God.
You do not need to confess private details publicly.
Someone else reading those words may be carrying the same struggle.
Your testimony might remind them that they are not alone.
And if this message brought conviction, please do not stop at emotion.
Open your Bible.
Read Deuteronomy 34 for yourself.
Read Numbers 20.
Read Hebrews 3.
Read the Transfiguration accounts.
Let Scripture test everything you hear, including this article.
Because our goal at Gospel Warrior is not to make people dependent upon powerful stories.
It is to help people become deeply rooted in the Word of God and personally devoted to Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, understand biblical truth, and walk with Christ beyond the momentary emotion of a social media post.
You do not.
Rather, because voluntarily supporting Gospel-centered discipleship can be one practical expression of Christian generosity and partnership in the work of sharing biblical truth.
Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive support (1 Corinthians 9:14), while also teaching that giving should be willing rather than compelled (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Whether you consider it part of your personal giving is a matter for prayerful stewardship and the teaching of your local church; it is not automatically a biblical tithe.
Those products can serve as reminders of Scripture, opportunities to encourage others, and tools for faith-centered conversations.
But the deeper invitation is not about merchandise.
It is about participating in the ongoing work of helping people encounter biblical truth.
A friend who is grieving.
A father who feels like a failure.
A mother who has been praying for years.
A believer struggling with shame.
A person who has never understood the difference between religion and the grace of Jesus Christ.
You may never know who reads it because you shared it.
You may never see the conversation it starts.
You may never hear the prayer someone whispers after encountering the Scriptures.
But sharing truth with love is worthwhile even when its results remain unseen.
Not every testimony needs to be dramatic.
Sometimes the words “God kept me through it” are enough to give another person courage.
There stands Moses.
An old servant of God.
Looking toward the land.
His strength not yet diminished, according to Deuteronomy 34:7, though the end of his earthly life has arrived.
The promise is before him.
The boundary remains.
The next generation will continue.
And somewhere beyond the final recorded moments of his life, there is a grave whose location will not be preserved for the world.
No monument necessary.
No pilgrimage required.
No human applause able to add anything to the faithfulness of God.
And centuries later, when Moses appears with Elijah on the mountain of Transfiguration, the voice of the Father directs attention not to Moses, but to Jesus.
“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him.” (Matthew 17:5, KJV)
Hear Him.
That is where the story leads.
Not to a hidden grave.
Not to a dead prophet's reputation.
But to the living Christ.
The One who fulfilled the Law.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who was buried and rose again.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His blood.
The One who does not promise that every earthly dream will come true, but promises eternal life to those who believe in Him.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because your life has not unfolded the way you hoped, remember this:
A closed earthly door is not proof that God's love has ended.
A painful consequence does not mean repentance is pointless.
An unfinished dream does not make an entire life meaningless.
And an unknown grave does not mean an unknown servant.
Bring your failures to Jesus.
Bring your disappointments.
Bring the bitterness you have hidden.
Bring the pride you have defended.
Bring the exhaustion of trying to be remembered.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Because the greatest ending is not having the world remember your name.
It is belonging forever to the Savior whose name is above every name.
Moses' story reminds us that even great servants reach the end of their earthly assignments.
But Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.
And that is why our message will always return to grace.
Not cheap grace that excuses sin.
But costly grace purchased through the blood of Christ.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that transforms.
Grace that teaches us to deny ungodliness.
Grace that turns our eyes away from our own monuments and toward the glory of God.
Grace that meets repentant sinners in the ruins of their choices and gives them a new life in Christ.
The world may never know where you were laid to rest, but if you belong to Jesus, death will never make Him lose sight of you.
